title: 'Excited delirium' training needed: judge
article: Front line emergency workers across Alberta should be trained to recognize and respond to people suffering from "excited delirium," according to a fatality inquiry into the death of a man in police custody.

Excited delirium came to the fore this month after RCMP officers shocked Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski with a Taser at Vancouver airport and the man died. RCMP speculated Dziekanski may have died from the rare condition, sometimes seen in people who are highly agitated or under the influence of stimulants while being restrained by police.

Hearing an inquiry into the death of Rocky Mountain House man Ted Meiorin, who died in mid-2006 without ever being Tasered, Judge Monica Rae Bast said better education and awareness could "potentially prevent some deaths from excited delirium."
In the report released this week, she recommended training physicians, EMS personnel, law enforcement personnel and dispatchers for EMS and the police.

Under Bast's recommendations, a list of signs of excited delirium would be established, as would separate protocols for each group of front line professionals to follow when they encounter people who display signs of the condition.
Bast, who also reviewed the Chief Medical Examiner of Alberta's finding on Meiorin's death, agreed the man had died from cocaine- induced excited delirium.
Bystanders had called police to Meiorin's aid the night he died after seeing him run down the street clad in only boxer shorts and foaming at the mouth, saying, "They're out to get me".
When police arrived at Pillars Restaurant, where Meiorin was waiting, the man was agitated, sweating and breathing heavily, police said.
Meiorin allegedly threatened to kill the two police officers attending and was put face-first on the floor and handcuffed with his hands behind his back.
Minutes after Meiorin was placed in a sitting recovery position, police noticed he had stopped breathing.
Toxicology tests found 1.4mg/l to 1.6mg/l of cocaine and cocaine metabolites in Meiorin's system. Over 1.0 mg/l is considered life threatening, depending upon a person's tolerance to cocaine.
An autopsy revealed no brain injuries or natural diseases that could have caused Meiorin's death, but found some external bruising and minor cuts.

Emergency medical specialist Dr. Christine Hall, who specializes in excited delirium, told the inquiry that people with the condition often exhibited incoherence, were hot to the touch and could exhibit a lack of purposeful activity or random violence and destruction.
They were often found to be wearing little or no clothing.
She said people showing signs of excited delirium were often attracted to glass surfaces, such as windows and mirrors, and failed to respond normally to outside stimuli.
In recent years, police have cited "excited delirium" as the probable cause of death in a string of Taser-related deaths, including the case of Red Deer man Jason Doan.
Doan, who died in 2006, was allegedly smashing vehicle windows when police were called and subdued him using a Taser.
The Alberta Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has announced it will hold a public inquiry into Doan's death, but a date is yet to be set.
